query: Consider the following context: High-entropy alloy (HEA) multilayers represent a promising class of advanced coating materials due to their superior mechanical properties, corrosion resistance, and irradiation tolerance. However, the specific role of interface coherency on the creep behavior of HEA multilayers remains unclear. In that context, which material can be used for transition between diffusion-mediated and dislocation-mediated creep mechanisms, and why?

generation.hypothesis: In HEA multilayers, inserting a thin tungsten (W) interfacial layer will create a controlled interface coherency that serves as an effective transition between regimes of diffusion-mediated creep at lower temperatures and dislocation-mediated creep at higher temperatures.
generation.material_initial_state: HEA multilayer coatings with coherent interfaces between layers
generation.intervention: Introduce a tungsten (W) transition layer (of nanoscale thickness) at the interfaces between HEA layers
generation.conditions: Experiments conducted across a range of temperatures and applied stresses that span both the diffusion creep regime (low-temperature/low-stress) and the dislocation creep regime (high-temperature/high-stress)
generation.structural_mediator: Modification of interface coherency by the tungsten layer, which adjusts the lattice mismatch between the HEA layers
generation.mechanism: The tungsten interlayer, due to its high melting point and atomic size, stabilizes coherent interfaces at lower temperatures, thereby limiting dislocation nucleation and favoring diffusion-mediated creep; as temperature and stress increase, thermal activation reduces the interface coherency, facilitating dislocation motion and transition to dislocation-mediated creep.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to HEA multilayers without a tungsten interlayer, the tungsten-modified interfaces will exhibit a measurable decrease in creep rate in the diffusion-controlled regime followed by a pronounced switch to dislocation activity at higher temperatures, as observed through changes in dislocation density and creep strain rates.
generation.baseline: HEA multilayers fabricated without an engineered tungsten transition layer, where the creep mechanism transition is less distinct or uncontrolled.
generation.boundary: The effectiveness of the tungsten layer may depend on its thickness and the specific HEA composition; if the tungsten layer is too thick or if testing conditions are outside the targeted temperature/stress range, the expected transition might not occur.
generation.uncertainty: While tungsten is predicted to modulate interface coherency effectively, the precise quantitative effects on the rate and exact temperature–stress conditions for the transition remain uncertain and need systematic experimental quantification.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of HEA multilayer samples: one with engineered tungsten interfacial layers and one without. Subject both sets to a series of creep tests over a controlled temperature and stress range. Use high-resolution TEM to assess interface coherency and quantify dislocation structures at various stages of creep.
measurements: Creep strain vs. time under constant stress at different temperatures
Interface coherence measurements using high-resolution electron microscopy
Comparison of creep rate transitions between the two sample sets
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the tungsten interlayer does not result in a statistically significant change in the creep behavior (i.e., no clear transition from diffusion-mediated to dislocation-mediated creep compared to the baseline sample) or if interface coherency remains unchanged, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) have excellent mechanical properties, which could make them the substitutes of some superalloys. However, the high melting point of refractory HEAs leads to processing problems when using traditional processing techniques. In this study, a single BCC solid solution of NbMoTaW alloy was formed by selective laser melting (SLM) with a linear energy density of up to 2.83 J/mm. The composition distribution was analyzed, and the element with a lower melting point and lower density showed a negative deviation (no more than 5%) of the molar ratio in the formed alloy. The HEA shows an excellent microstructure, microhardness, and corrosion resistance performance compared with traditional superalloys, making it a new substitute metal with great application prospects in aerospace and energy fields.
